segments.title: When an archive visit costs less than ordering photographs
segments.body: Archive travel and photographs are among the remaining costs of completing the planned naval-history primers. The Historiophon fundraiser is intended to cover research visits and obtain the images needed to finish the books. For two proposed trips, visiting the collections in person would cost substantially less than asking them to supply photographs remotely. Travel can therefore be the cheaper way to obtain a book's illustrations.

evidence.note: Fundraising for primer research and photographs, including two archive visits expected to cost substantially less than obtaining the photographs remotely.

segments.summary: Two planned archive visits would cost less than obtaining photographs remotely, making travel part of the illustration budget for the naval-history primers.

segments.title: Naval-history primers, archive access, and global coverage
segments.body: The planned primers are illustrated introductions of about 45,000 words to a ship class, person, or naval subject, intended for Kindle. British subjects come first because they are more affordable for the author to research. Longer-term interests include Japanese and American subjects, South American ships and senior officers, and Indian naval officers since independence. The proposed Indian subjects are of particular interest for their innovative ideas and perceived lack of coverage for English-speaking audiences. Wider coverage would involve visits to archives around the world, although the prospect of visiting Russian archives remains uncertain.

evidence.note: The 45,000-word primer format, the financial reasons for beginning with British subjects, and longer-term interest in overseas archives, South American ships and officers, and Indian officers since independence.

segments.summary: The planned primer series begins with British subjects to keep initial research costs down, with later studies intended to cover officers and ships from other navies.

segments.title: When a leadership profile requires archival research
segments.body: A viewer-nominated commander may be difficult to research if regular books, existing profiles, and accessible autobiographical material provide no usable account. Preparing a leadership profile would then require an archive search for sources about the person's career. Such work cannot be promised within the Christmas series' schedule. A nominee needing that research would probably move to a later series, allowing time to look for the material before making the video.

evidence.note: Commanders lacking accessible profiles or autobiographical sources require an archive search and would probably be considered for a later series.

segments.summary: A commander absent from readily available biographical sources may need an archive search, putting a profile beyond the Christmas series' schedule.

segments.title: Using history streams to support small maritime museums
segments.body: The 2024 Historiophon is intended to test whether a long history stream can raise enough money to interest small naval and maritime museums in future partnerships. The proposed arrangement would split incoming funds equally between a museum and the organiser. The organiser's share could cover the material delivered, research trips, or pictures for books. Museums would first need evidence that the event could generate worthwhile income. If the model worked, it could become a regular Christmas fundraiser, with the hope that other historians and YouTube educators would adopt it too.

evidence.note: A proposed 50-50 museum partnership, the need to demonstrate fundraising income, and the hope that other historians and educators would adopt the format.

segments.summary: The 2024 Historiophon would test whether a long history stream could become a recurring fundraiser shared with small naval and maritime museums.

segments.title: The ethical case for paying archive-image fees consistently
segments.body: Four required image sets come from a particularly expensive source that alone holds them. The ethical argument for paying its charges rests on applying the same standard to large institutions and small collections. Working around an expensive institution's criteria could give someone else a justification for avoiding the modest charges of a smaller collection that needs the income. Paying consistently is the proposed way to defend small collections' claims to payment. That standard rests on respecting someone else's property, even when the price seems excessive.

evidence.note: Four image sets held by an expensive sole source, and the ethical argument that paying its charges supports a consistent standard for small collections too.

segments.summary: The case for paying licensed archive-image fees rests on treating large institutions and small collections by the same ethical standard.
